title: A victory over biker criminals
article: The mighty are falling in Quebec, where Hells Angels biker gang leader Maurice ("Mom") Boucher was convicted on the weekend of the 1997 shooting murders of two prison guards.

Boucher's jury conviction was a historic triumph for Quebec justice, a province where biker gangs operate like the old-style Mafia, murdering, extorting and dealing in drugs and prostitution. In the past, witnesses and jurors in other gang members' court cases have been intimidated, paralysing the justice system. This time, it is the bikers who have been stunned.
Boucher's case illustrates just how dangerous the biker underworld really is. And Quebec is just getting a handle on the problem. About 75 Hells Angels members are now in jail awaiting trial.

Taking into consideration all the violence associated with biker gangs, it was upsetting to see in the April 29 Whig-Standard a photo of four Bandidos members standing at a booth at the Kingston Memorial Centre motorcycle show, pictured beneath a sign reading: "Support Your Local Bandidos."
Support them in what? Dealing drugs? Pimping? Killing people? What is their business or pleasure?
And what prompted motorcycle show organizers to allow such a display? These aren't motorcycle salespeople. These are men promoting a criminal lifestyle.

Kingston should not tolerate such displays, especially since a Hells Angels associate, Daniel Lamer, was gunned down by police on Highway 401 in March as he was travelling to Kingston, allegedly to kill a Kingston Bandido. Kingston is becoming a centre of biker activity, which was proven when about 100 Bandidos gathered here in December to celebrate the end of the local chapter's probationary period.

Convictions such as Boucher's help dispel notions of biker gangs being mere brotherhoods or social clubs. The 1997 Quebec prison guard murders were terrible. As the Quebec court heard, Boucher ordered the killings of the guards as part of a wider plot to intimidate the provincial justice system. Next on his list were police officers, prosecutors and judges.

The men and women who sat on the Boucher jury are to be congratulated for showing courage in delivering the guilty verdict. Past juries have been intimidated by bikers, and some jurors have been paid by the gangs to interfere with justice and push for acquittals.
In this case, an opaque screen blocked the view of the jury from the courtroom. Any person wearing biker logos or tattoos had to cover them up. And jurors' names were not released to the public.
Deliberating under such extreme conditions and pressures, these people did well to stand up and deliver justice on behalf of all their fellow citizens.

Already, biker gang members outside Quebec are putting their spin on the Boucher verdict and biker gangs in general. They say that Quebec gangs are the most violent and that Boucher was the most bloodthirsty of all in his attempts to take over the drug trade. But if the March shootout on Highway 401 is an indicator, the Kingston Bandidos "brotherhood" that asks for our "support" is active enough to prompt a killing by their Hells Angels rivals.
Bloody shootouts and anonymous juries are not the kind of future Kingstonians should support.
